units.title: Unit 23 — Festivals and celebrations
learningObjectives: Use idiomatic phrases for festival dates, traditions, seasonal events and public celebrations.
Distinguish preserving traditions from breaking with them, and recognise the figurative use of movable feast.
Choose natural wedding expressions with suitable informal, ceremonial or humorous register.
Avoid treating dress as a countable noun when it refers to a clothing style.

items.pt: um festival cai em determinada data
items.example: This year's lantern festival falls on the first Friday in November.
items.note: A festival falls on a date when it takes place then; fall on also works for birthdays and public holidays.

items.example: The coastal town will hold an annual festival devoted to traditional storytelling.
items.note: Hold a festival means organise and host the event; annual means once every year.

items.example: The neighbourhood gathers every autumn to celebrate a tradition started by its first residents.
items.note: Celebrate a tradition highlights actively honouring an established custom.

items.example: The new organisers promised to uphold a tradition of inviting local musicians.
items.note: Uphold a tradition means maintain a valued custom, sometimes despite pressure to abandon it.

items.example: Families continue to keep up an age-old tradition of lighting candles at dusk.
items.note: Age-old is literary or journalistic for very old; keep up means continue a practice.

items.example: The town's harvest ceremony may date back to the early nineteenth century.
items.note: Date back to identifies the period when a custom or institution began; it takes a time expression.

items.example: Visitors are welcome to join in the festivities after the parade ends.
items.note: Join in the festivities means participate in the celebration, rather than merely watch it.

items.example: By sunset the entire neighbourhood seemed to be in a festive mood.
items.note: Festive mood describes a cheerful atmosphere associated with celebration; in festive mood also occurs in British English.

items.example: The opening dance will mark the beginning of the week-long celebration.
items.note: Mark the beginning means symbolise or officially signal the start of a period or event.

items.pt: a época de festas de fim de ano
items.example: Restaurants usually become much busier as the festive season approaches.
items.note: The festive season often refers particularly to Christmas and New Year, depending on cultural context.

items.example: Local teenagers will perform a traditional dance at the cultural fair.
items.note: Perform naturally combines with dance when describing a public presentation.

items.example: The procession included dancers wearing traditional dress from the mountain villages.
items.note: Dress is uncountable when it means a style of clothing; traditional dresses means individual garments for women.

items.example: Decorating the town square has become an annual tradition for the volunteers.
items.note: An annual tradition is a custom repeated each year, unlike a one-off celebration.

items.example: Because the date follows a lunar calendar, the observance is a movable feast.
items.note: A movable feast is a religious holiday with a changing date; figuratively it can mean a flexible arrangement.

items.example: The island has a rich tradition of oral history and folk music.
items.note: A rich tradition suggests an extensive, valuable cultural history, not financial wealth.

items.example: The museum works with residents to protect the area's cultural heritage.
items.note: Cultural heritage refers to shared traditions, arts and practices passed between generations.

items.example: The council plans to put on a firework display after the outdoor concert.
items.note: Put on means organise or present a public event; firework display names the spectacle.

items.example: The school has a proud tradition of welcoming students from different backgrounds.
items.note: A proud tradition describes a long-standing practice that a community values.

items.pt: celebrar ou cumprir as tradições de uma festividade
items.example: Several families will observe a festival through prayer and communal meals.
items.note: Observe a festival can mean celebrate or follow its religious and cultural customs; it is relatively formal.

items.example: Choosing a contemporary dance troupe was a deliberate break with tradition.
items.note: A break with tradition means a departure from established custom, not a temporary pause in festivities.

items.example: The association has a long-standing tradition of hosting free community meals.
items.note: Long-standing describes an established custom that has existed for many years.

items.pt: arrecadar recursos para uma causa beneficente
items.example: Volunteers sold handmade decorations to raise funds for charity.
items.note: Raise funds for charity means collect money for a charitable purpose, often through events.

items.word: a display of traditional arts and crafts
items.pt: uma exposição de artes e artesanato tradicionais
items.example: The library organised a display of traditional arts and crafts by regional makers.
items.note: Put on or organise a display are natural combinations for presenting an exhibition.

items.example: The festive season gets underway when the main square's lights are switched on.
items.note: Get underway means begin, often used in announcements and reports of organised events.

items.example: The bride's sister volunteered to make a speech after dinner.
items.note: Make a speech is neutral and works at weddings and formal occasions; give a speech is also natural.

items.example: After many years together, the couple finally decided to get hitched.
items.note: Get hitched is informal for get married and may sound playful in a wedding speech.

items.example: The couple plan to tie the knot in a small ceremony by the sea.
items.note: Tie the knot is an informal idiom for getting married, not simply becoming engaged.

items.example: Even experienced public speakers can suffer from pre-wedding nerves.
items.note: Pre-wedding nerves are feelings of anxiety before the ceremony; pre-wedding jitters is informal too.

items.example: The celebrant invited the pair to be joined in matrimony before their families.
items.note: Be joined in matrimony is a formal, ceremonial expression for marriage, unlike get hitched.

items.example: At the reception, the grandmother stood up to propose a toast to the newlyweds.
items.note: Propose a toast introduces words of goodwill before people drink in someone's honour.

items.pt: erguer as taças para um brinde
items.example: The host called out, "Raise your glasses," before thanking the guests.
items.note: Raise your glasses is a conventional invitation during a toast; with third-person subjects use raise their glasses.

items.example: Their friends wished them a lifetime of wedded bliss during the reception.
items.note: Wedded bliss means happiness in marriage and often has a lightly humorous tone.

items.example: The youngest guest was delighted to make a toast at the anniversary party.
items.note: A toast is a countable ceremonial expression of goodwill; uncountable toast means browned bread.

items.example: Guests were asked to wear formal dress for the awards ceremony.
items.note: Formal dress refers to a style or dress code and is uncountable in this meaning.

units.title: Unit 24 — Cosmetics and fashion
learningObjectives: Understand frequent skincare and beauty-advertising collocations without confusing promotional claims with verified results.
Use idiomatic terms for fashionable clothing, retail availability, trend-setting and seasonal collections.
Recognise British English expressions such as high-street fashion, hit the high street and feel peckish.
Distinguish the intensity and register of descriptive combinations such as flawless complexion and excruciatingly uncomfortable.

items.example: The new hair dye promises long-lasting colour after several washes.
items.note: Long-lasting describes an effect that remains for an extended period; it is common in cosmetics advertising.

items.example: A gentle conditioner may help improve the appearance of sun-damaged hair.
items.note: Sun-damaged modifies hair affected by sun exposure; it does not mean naturally light-coloured hair.

items.example: The advertisement highlights the serum's supposed anti-aging properties.
items.note: Anti-aging properties is promotional language; the phrase alone does not demonstrate a product's effectiveness.

items.example: The company described its formula as clinically proven but provided no study details.
items.note: Clinically proven is a strong evidence claim used in advertising; verify supporting research rather than accepting the wording alone.

items.example: The poster boldly claimed that its cream could banish wrinkles within a month.
items.note: Banish wrinkles is vivid promotional language suggesting complete removal, not a neutral scientific description.

items.example: The boutique introduced a luxury cream in a small glass container.
items.note: Luxury modifies a premium product and often conveys exclusivity rather than proven superiority.

items.example: The makeup artist applied concealer carefully around the fine lines near her eyes.
items.note: Fine lines are small facial creases and are a standard collocation in skincare language.

items.example: Digital editing gave the portrait an almost flawless complexion.
items.note: Flawless complexion is a strong beauty description; advertisements may use it aspirationally.

items.example: The café offers tasty snacks for passengers with little time to eat.
items.note: Tasty commonly describes pleasant-flavoured food, including light snacks.

items.example: If you feel peckish before dinner, there is fruit on the kitchen table.
items.note: Feel peckish is informal, especially British English, for feeling slightly hungry.

items.example: The resort claims to provide unrivalled service to every guest.
items.note: Unrivalled is a strong promotional superlative implying that no competitor matches the service.

items.example: A new exclusive beauty salon has opened inside the historic hotel.
items.note: Exclusive suggests restricted access, high-end positioning or prestige, depending on context.

items.example: The stylist chose a gentle rinse to bring out natural highlights in her hair.
items.note: Bring out means make an existing quality more noticeable; highlights are lighter strands or tones.

items.example: The nutrition label describes the fortified cereal as rich in vitamin D.
items.note: Rich in names a relatively high amount of a nutrient; substantive health claims need evidence.

items.example: The product page promises instant results, although customers should check the evidence.
items.note: Instant results is persuasive advertising language for effects claimed to appear immediately.

items.pt: recuperar a aparência de cabelos danificados pelo sol
items.example: The salon advertises a treatment intended to revive sun-damaged hair.
items.note: Revive hair is promotional wording for improving its appearance or condition, not literally bringing it back to life.

items.example: The travel guide features exclusive spas offering private treatment rooms.
items.note: Exclusive spas suggests prestigious or restricted-access wellness facilities.

items.example: The nail polish is available in a range of long-lasting colours.
items.note: A range of introduces a selection; long-lasting describes how well the colour remains.

items.word: subtly bring out the natural highlights
items.example: A clear gloss can subtly bring out the natural highlights in darker hair.
items.note: Subtly modifies bring out to suggest a gentle rather than dramatic visual effect.

items.example: She spent the afternoon browsing glossy magazines at the airport bookshop.
items.note: Glossy magazines are photo-heavy publications on coated paper, often covering fashion and celebrity culture.

items.example: Brightly coloured scarves are in fashion again this autumn.
items.note: In fashion means currently fashionable; it contrasts with out of fashion.

items.example: He preferred second-hand jackets to expensive designer label clothes.
items.note: Designer label clothes refers to garments sold under recognised fashion designers' brands.

items.pt: moda de lojas populares de rua
items.example: The exhibition explores how high-street fashion responds to runway designs.
items.note: High-street fashion is a British English term for clothes sold by mainstream retail chains.

items.example: The independent brand plans to launch a new collection in early spring.
items.note: Launch a collection is the established expression for introducing a new clothing range to the market.

items.example: Pastel jackets are central to the new season's look in the designer's campaign.
items.note: The new season's look describes the overall fashion style promoted for the coming season.

items.example: A small local label managed to set the trend for recycled denim.
items.note: Set the trend means establish a style that other people then follow.

items.example: The shop unveiled a stunning range of locally made accessories.
items.note: Stunning range combines an enthusiastic adjective with a selection of products.

items.pt: chegar às lojas do comércio popular
items.example: The recycled-fabric coats are expected to hit the high street next month.
items.note: Hit the high street means become available through mainstream shops, especially in British English.

items.example: The relaxed linen outfit became a hugely popular look during the summer.
items.note: Hugely intensifies popular; look refers to a recognisable clothing style.

items.example: He called himself a fashion victim after buying shoes that hurt his feet.
items.note: Fashion victim is usually disapproving or humorous for someone who follows trends despite poor fit or appearance.

items.example: The costume looked elegant but was excruciatingly uncomfortable to wear.
items.note: Excruciatingly is a very strong intensifier, appropriate for extreme discomfort rather than a minor annoyance.

items.example: Wide-leg trousers are back in fashion after several years away from the shops.
items.note: Back in fashion means a previously popular style has become fashionable again.

items.example: The photographer has covered fashion shows in several European cities.
items.note: Fashion show is the conventional noun phrase for an event presenting designers' clothing.

items.example: The boutique sells several designer labels alongside locally made accessories.
items.note: Designer labels are fashion brands associated with named designers; this does not mean clothing size labels.

items.example: The online shop released a summer collection featuring lightweight fabrics.
items.note: Summer collection names clothing designed or marketed for a particular season.

items.example: The travel agent suggested a classy hotel near the concert hall.
items.note: Classy is an approving, relatively informal adjective for elegance or quality.
